Light Air Sealing — Executive Summary

The goal of this work is to develop energy efficiency, demand flexibility, and other retrofit enduse load shapes (electricity, gas, propane, or fuel oil) that cover the majority of high-impact, market-ready (or nearly market-ready) measures. 'Measures' refers to retrofits that can be applied to buildings during modeling.

An 'end-use savings shape' is the difference in energy consumption between a baseline building and a building with an energy efficiency, demand flexibility, or other retrofit measure applied. It results in a time-series profile that is broken down by end use and fuel (electricity or on-site gas, propane, or fuel oil use) at each time step.

ResStock™ is a highly granular, physics-based, bottom-up model that uses multiple data sources, statistical sampling methods, and advanced building energy simulations to estimate the annual subhourly energy consumption of the residential building stock across the United States. The baseline model intends to represent the U.S. residential building stock as it existed in 2018. Technical documentation for the inputs and assumptions in the baseline building stock model is available in Reyna et al. (2025). Calibration and validation of the baseline model results are available in the final technical report of the End-Use Load Profiles project (Wilson et al. 2022).

This documentation focuses on a single end-use savings shape measure: Light Air Sealing .

This upgrade demonstrated 6% modeled total site energy savings (166 TWh) for the U.S. residential building stock (see Figure 3 for details). These savings are primarily attributed to:

- 11% stock natural gas heating savings (103 TWh)
- 10% stock electricity heating savings (21 TWh)
- 11% stock fuel oil heating savings (15 TWh)
- 11% stock propane heating savings (11 TWh).

Light Air Sealing — 1  Technology Summary

Air sealing involves identifying and closing large and small gaps, cracks, and penetrations in the home's primary or secondary pressure boundaries, such as around windows, doors, attic hatches, and plumbing or wiring holes (U.S. Department of Energy 2025). These leaks, whether large or small, accumulate and can allow a substantial amount of heated or cooled air to escape. By reducing air leaks, air sealing improves indoor comfort, maintains more stable temperatures, and reduces the workload on the heating and cooling system. Air sealing is especially important in older homes, which typically have more leaks (Green Building Alliance 2025). For a comprehensive overview of air sealing and the technology in general, see ResStock Measure Documentation: Advanced Air Sealing (Brossman, White and Phoung 2026).

Light Air Sealing — 1.1  Technical Measure Details

Only dwelling units that have an infiltration rate of 10 ACH50 or greater are assumed to be applicable for this 'Light Air Sealing' measure. That is because this ResStock measure does not add mechanical ventilation to dwelling units with a low infiltration rate. Whole-home mechanical ventilation should be considered when the infiltration rate is 5 ACH50 or less according to the 2015 International Residential Code (ICC Digital Codes 2024). This 10 ACH50 cutoff is due to natural ventilation requirements that homes generally receive at least 0.35 air changes per hour (ASHRAE 2016, International Code Council 2021). 1 A 25% reduction in infiltration of a 10 ACH50 dwelling will reduce its ACH50 value to 7.5 ACH50. The 'LBL factor' (developed by Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory) is a factor based on climate region and other characteristics, and is used to convert estimated air changes in a building by natural means without a fan to the air changes per hour at 50 Pa (ACH50). Using an LBL factor of 20, the lowest allowable infiltration level without forcing natural ventilation into the house is 7 ACH50 (ENERGY STAR 2001).

1 At least 0.35 air changes per hour, but not less than 15 cubic feet of air per minute per person (International Code Council 2021). See ASHRAE 2016 for the specific requirements and equations for calculating required ventilation.

Light Air Sealing — 3  Modeling Approach

Previous air sealing modeling in ResStock covers how residential air infiltration is modeled (Phoung, Lou and White 2026). ResStock models residential air infiltration values expressed as ACH50. Each dwelling unit in the ResStock dataset is assigned an existing ACH50 value based on housing stock characteristics, informed by the Residential Diagnostics Database (ResDB). ResStock integrates this information using probabilistic sampling logic to represent the diversity of the U.S. housing stock. These infiltration rates are dependent on climate zone, floor area, and vintage. In ResStock, the current infiltration values are based on single-family detached blower door tests in units of ACH50. For single-family detached homes, the ACH50 values reflect total leakage to the outdoors, and buffer zones such as unconditioned attics, crawlspaces, and garages. However, for multifamily and single-family attached units, ResStock models leakage as total unit air leakage, which includes airflow to both the exterior and adjacent units. To estimate only the leakage to the exterior, the model scales the total sampled ACH50 by the ratio of the exteriorfacing envelope area to the total envelope area. This adjusted exterior-only infiltration rate is then used in the simulation outputs. Electrical panel constraint modeling was added to ResStock via OpenStudio-HPXML measures in 2025 to assess whether the existing panel has enough capacity or breaker space to accommodate new loads from an energy retrofit. For details on panel constraint modeling, refer to the ResStock Technical Reference Guide (Reyna, et al. 2025). This measure does not introduce new electrical loads or circuits, so it has no impact on the electrical panel. Any panel constraints appearing in the upgrade results reflect pre-existing conditions, as this measure does not worsen them.

Light Air Sealing — 3.1  OpenStudio-HPXML Overview

ResStock relies heavily on the OpenStudio-HPXML workflow, and the general steps are as follows:

- -Step 1: Build probability distributions for housing characteristics in the energy model
- -Step 2: Apply custom ResStock model arguments to the energy model
- -Step 3: Fill in energy model assumptions using BuildResidentialHPXML
- -Step 4: Fill in appliance and occupant schedule assumptions using BuildResidentialScheduleFile
- -Step 5: Use the OpenStudio-HPXML workflow to change the building energy model to a HPXML file and then model the dwelling unit

For in-depth information about the ResStock modeling workflow, including repository version tags, housing characteristic distribution examples, sampling descriptions, and model articulation, see the Version History and the Workflow sections of the Technical Reference Guide from the ResStock 2025 Release 1, which is unchanged for this ResStock 2025 Release 2 (Reyna, et al. 2025).

Light Air Sealing — 3.2  Air Sealing

In ResStock, building characteristics are translated to OS-HPXML parameters using the options\_lookup.tsv file. Measure upgrades, such as infiltration, are modeled as changes to baseline building characteristics. This section outlines the technical details of how infiltration upgrades are implemented in the ResStock workflow.

Light Air Sealing — ResStock Inputs for the Light Air Sealing Upgrade

Table 3 summarizes the inputs associated with the infiltration upgrade (air sealing) in ResStock (Phoung, Lou and White 2026). These inputs are passed to OS-HPXML to generate the corresponding HPXML files for the simulation. In cases where infiltration details (ACH50) are not explicitly defined in ResStock, default values (Table 3) are assigned by OS-HPXML based on building characteristics.

Table 3. ResStock Argument Values for Infiltration Options

text:
Light Air Sealing — Default Inputs from OpenStudio-HPXML for Infiltration Upgrade

The ResStock inputs in the table above are sent to OS-HPXML. Any values that are not specified by ResStock are calculated using the defaults in the BuildResidentialHPXML OpenStudio measure based on building characteristics. These characteristics include the building's floor area, number of stories, vintage, ceiling height, duct locations, foundation type, and climate zone. Other characteristics include stack effect, indoor-outdoor temperature difference, wind speed, and more. In multifamily and attached buildings, OS-HPXML assumes that some air leakage occurs between units rather than solely to the outside. To account for this, the software adjusts total infiltration based on the portion of the building envelope that is exposed to the exterior. More details of the infiltration model and default values can be found in the Alberta Air Infiltration Model (AIM-2) (Walker and Wilson 1990).

The Connecticut model shows an annual site energy reduction of 5.9% from the light air sealing measure. This model shows higher annual cooling savings (15.8%) compared to annual heating savings (9.5%). The cooling and heating hourly peak power shows minimal decrease, at 1.4% and 1.8%, respectively.

The Florida model shows a 7.2% decrease in annual site energy, with annual cooling and heating energy consumption decreasing by 6.8% and 15.2%, respectively. The cooling peak power is reduced by 4.5%, and heating hourly peak power is reduced by 10.3%.

The Texas model shows an annual site energy decrease of 7.4%. Annual cooling and heating consumptions both decrease, with cooling savings of 8.7% and heating savings of 19%. Annual hourly peak cooling and heating power both decrease, by 0.9% and 10.9%, respectively. In both the Texas and Florida models, the annual heating energy shows a higher percent decrease than annual cooling energy. These models have minimal heating requirements, and therefore the percent change in heating energy is more sensitive. By magnitude, the annual heating savings is comparable or smaller than the annual cooling savings.

Light Air Sealing — 4.4  Stock Energy Impacts

Out of 550,000 dwelling models (i.e., the total number of units modeled in the ResStock 2025 Release 1 dataset to represent the national building stock), 426,800 models (77.6%) are applicable for the light air sealing upgrade. For the 426,800 applicable models, the total weighted baseline modeled site energy consumption is 2,664 TWh per year. After applying the light air sealing upgrade, the total modeled site consumption was reduced to 2,498 TWh per year, a 6.2% reduction. Figure 3 shows that energy savings from light air sealing primarily come from heating and cooling end uses, with 11% natural gas heating savings (104 TWh), 10% electricity heating savings (21 TWh), 11% fuel oil heating savings (15 TWh), 11% propane heating savings (11 TWh), and 3% electricity cooling savings (8 TWh). Other end uses like lighting and appliances remained unchanged or very minimally impacted.

Light Air Sealing — 4.4  Stock Energy Impacts

heating savings (15 TWh), 11% propane heating savings (11 TWh), and 3% electricity cooling savings (8 TWh). Other end uses like lighting and appliances remained unchanged or very minimally impacted.

Reasoning for these results was provided in previous air sealing work (Phoung, Lou and White 2026) and is restated here. Air sealing improves building performance by reducing air leakage. Thus, its impact is confined to systems that respond to indoor temperature fluctuations. The heating and cooling energy savings can be attributed to reduced air infiltration, which limits the amount of cold or hot outdoor air entering the building envelope during the heating or cooling season, respectively. This leads to lower heating and cooling loads, reduced runtime for space heating and cooling systems, and associated reductions in fan and pump operation.

percent savings observed in 7A (9%), 6A (8%), and 5A (7%). This is primarily due to large heating loads in these climates and the greater temperature differentials that drive infiltration losses.

Climate zones with moisture classification A (moist) typically exhibit higher energy savings compared to climate zones with moisture classifications B (dry) or C (marine). In moist climates, infiltration air contains more humidity, requiring HVAC systems to expend additional energy to remove both sensible and latent heat. In contrast, dry climates have minimal latent loads, and marine climates generally experience more moderate temperatures, resulting in lower overall energy use associated with conditioning infiltration air. Therefore, improving infiltration will have greater effect in moist climates and demonstrate higher savings.

Figure 12 shows that heating savings consistently exceed cooling savings across most climate zones, except for climate zone 1A. Infiltration has much greater effect on heating loads because the temperature difference between the outside and indoor air is typically much higher during winter (e.g., 20°F outdoor vs. 70°F indoor during winter, compared with 90°F outdoor vs. 70°F indoor during summer). Therefore, an air sealing upgrade is expected to have much higher effect on heating energy consumption.
